lesson.title: The Electrons Left Behind: Lone Pairs in Lewis Structures
lesson.summary: A lone pair is a pair of valence electrons that belongs to one atom and is not shared with another atom, and its presence shapes both molecular geometry and chemical reactivity.
lesson.body:
When you build a Lewis structure, valence electrons split into two categories: bonding pairs that are shared between two atoms, and lone pairs, sometimes called nonbonding pairs, which sit on a single atom and are not shared with any neighbor. Lone pairs are usually drawn as two dots next to an atom's symbol, and they count fully toward that one atom's octet even though they never form part of a bond.

Water, H2O, is a clear example. Oxygen brings 6 valence electrons and each hydrogen brings 1, for a total of 8. Oxygen forms two O-H single bonds, which uses 4 electrons, 2 per bond, leaving 4 electrons. Those 4 electrons become two lone pairs on the oxygen atom. Check the octet on oxygen: 2 electrons from each of its two bonds, 4 total, plus its two lone pairs, 4 total, equals 8. The two hydrogens each need only 2 electrons to be satisfied, which they get from their single shared bonding pair.

Ammonia, NH3, shows a molecule with just one lone pair on the central atom. Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons and each of the three hydrogens has 1, for a total of 8. Three N-H bonds use 6 electrons, leaving 1 lone pair, 2 electrons, on nitrogen. That single lone pair is chemically important: it is the reason ammonia acts as a base and readily donates its electron pair to a proton, H+, to form the ammonium ion, NH4+.

Lone pairs matter well beyond bookkeeping. Because a lone pair occupies space around a central atom without being pulled toward a second nucleus, it tends to spread out more than a bonding pair and pushes neighboring bonds closer together, which is why water's H-O-H angle, about 104.5 degrees, is noticeably smaller than the perfect tetrahedral angle of 109.5 degrees. Lone pairs also make an atom a Lewis base, a potential site for forming a new bond, and they are essential to correctly assigning formal charge, since an atom's formal charge calculation depends directly on how many nonbonding electrons it holds. This same repulsion effect explains why ammonia's H-N-H angle, about 107 degrees, sits between water's compressed angle and methane's perfect 109.5 degree angle: fewer lone pairs on the central atom means less compression of the bonding pairs. Chemists rank the strength of these repulsions as lone pair to lone pair greater than lone pair to bonding pair greater than bonding pair to bonding pair, a pattern you will use again once you study molecular geometry in more depth.

A useful habit when drawing any Lewis structure is to place bonds first to connect all atoms, then distribute the remaining valence electrons as lone pairs, starting with the outer atoms and finishing with the central atom, until every atom that needs an octet has one. Hydrogen, of course, needs only 2 electrons total and never gets a lone pair of its own once bonded. Recognizing which electrons are lone pairs and which are bonding pairs is the foundation for nearly every Lewis structure topic that follows, from formal charge to resonance to molecular shape.
